digest.intro: Sovereignty fractures everywhere — in cells, satellites, and state-level infrastructure.

items.title: The Kill Switch That Already Happened
items.blurb: Steve Blank, in London for a month, reports that the moment Elon Musk personally ordered Starshield throttled over Ukraine — not as U.S. policy, but apparently as a private decision — European policymakers stopped treating infrastructure dependency as a paranoid fantasy. The actual shift: conversations have moved from 'could this happen' to 'what do we build instead,' with urgency that hasn't existed in decades. One CEO, one decision, tilting a war — that's the new threat model.

items.title: Europe Eyes a Naval Operation in the Black Sea
items.blurb: The European Parliament passed a resolution calling for an EU naval operation in the Black Sea after Russian strikes on commercial vessels off Bulgaria and Romania — NATO members. This isn't rhetoric; it's the EU considering direct military presence in an active war zone's adjacent waters. The structural question is whether European institutions can move fast enough to matter before the posture hardens.

items.title: Open-Source 3D Printing at 9-Micron Resolution via Fiber Optics
items.blurb: The RepRapMicron project ran a UV LED through a trimmed single-mode fiber patch cord to cure SLA resin at roughly 9 µm resolution — small enough that a sneeze can lose the print forever. It's the RepRap philosophy (open, scavenged, iterative) applied to the microscopic: off-the-shelf optics doing work that normally requires a dedicated two-photon lithography rig. Overhangs are still a problem; everything else is genuinely impressive.

items.title: Was June 19, 1889 the Exact Night Van Gogh Painted The Starry Night?
items.blurb: Astronomers cross-referenced Venus's position in the painting against planetarium reconstructions of the sky visible from Saint-Rémy-de-Provence, then layered in historical weather records and — improbably — cicada activity as a temperature proxy to narrow the date. The Venus orb above the cypress tree has been confirmed as a real celestial observation; the new study tightens the previously agreed June 19 date with observational geometry nobody thought to apply before. It's the kind of problem where the discipline doing the work (astronomy) has no business solving it, which is exactly why they could.

items.title: LSD Speeds Up Brain Rhythms and Makes Them Fractal
items.blurb: A new small study challenges the prevailing 'default mode network suppression' model of how LSD works, finding instead that the drug accelerates certain brain rhythms and induces self-similar fractal patterns across timescales — the same mathematical structure that generates the kaleidoscopic visuals users report. It reframes psychedelics less as a 'turning off' of control systems and more as a reorganization of the brain's background hum into a different geometric regime. For anyone thinking about generative or recursive visual systems, this is a surprisingly literal connection.

items.title: Atomic Clocks Testing Einstein — And Finally Big Enough to Matter
items.blurb: Veritasium's best mode: explain why a precision instrument everyone assumes is settled actually sits at the live edge of physics. Modern atomic clocks are now sensitive enough to test whether gravity curves time the way general relativity predicts — and a device exists that could, for the first time, give the equivalence principle a real empirical run for its money. This channel has earned trust on exactly this kind of content.

facts.fact: A single-mode fiber patch cord trimmed with a hacksaw is all it takes to achieve 9-micron 3D print resolution in open-source RepRapMicron — the resulting prints are small enough to be destroyed by a breath.
Astronomers used historical cicada activity records as a temperature proxy to help pin the exact night Van Gogh painted The Starry Night.
LSD may induce fractal brain dynamics — self-similar patterns repeating across different timescales — rather than simply suppressing the default mode network as previously believed.

make_something.prompt: Build a generative piece that renders a night sky as Van Gogh might have painted it on June 19, 1889 — but drive the swirl parameters from real LSD-brain fractal data: self-similar turbulence patterns that repeat across spatial scales. Use the actual Venus position from planetarium records as a fixed anchor, and let the rest of the sky breathe with recursive noise at 2-3 octaves. The constraint: the cypress tree must be present, and the horizon must show light — Van Gogh painted it just before dawn.

art_picks.title: Sans Soleil
art_picks.creator: Chris Marker
art_picks.why: A film structured entirely around the gap between memory, image, and systems of meaning — Marker weaves footage from Japan, Guinea-Bissau, and Iceland into an essay on how cultures encode time and ritual. It's the kind of thing that rewires how you look at everything for weeks after.

art_picks.title: UUmwelt
art_picks.creator: Pierre Huyghe
art_picks.why: Freestanding screens across MoMA's Sculpture Garden display hallucinatory images generated by a neural network trained on fMRI brain-scan data — the machine's attempt to reconstruct a human thought. The installation responds in real time to visitor gaze via sensors, and to data from simulated cancer-cell mutations: three living systems in quiet dialogue. Closes November 29 — go before it's gone.

art_picks.title: Yanqui U.X.O.
art_picks.creator: Godspeed You! Black Emperor
art_picks.why: An album built like architecture — locked feedback loops, slow-moving systems of tension and release, field recordings braided into orchestral swells. The liner notes reveal the album's own structure as a diagram, which tells you everything about how obsessively these people work. For long studio sessions or deep listening.

events.name: Frisson Gallery: 2 x Self — Noah Pica & Paul Negron
events.venue: Frisson Gallery, 141 Attorney St, Lower East Side, Manhattan
events.why: A two-person show on self-representation at a small LES gallery that consistently programs work with formal rigor — the kind of spot worth knowing.

events.name: Synthesize Me: Olga Titus & Michael Dickey
events.venue: IRL Gallery, 86 Walker St #2, Tribeca, Manhattan
events.why: A two-person show at one of the more interesting small Tribeca spaces — the title alone suggests a dialogue between artists working across synthesis, material, and identity that's worth an afternoon detour.

events.name: Pierre Huyghe: UUmwelt
events.venue: MoMA Abby Aldrich Rockefeller Sculpture Garden, 11 W 53rd St, Manhattan
events.why: Machine learning meets brain-imaging data in an outdoor installation that responds to your gaze in real time — the rare show where the viewer is genuinely part of the system, not just a spectator.

events.name: Krasner–Pollock: Past Continuous
events.venue: The Metropolitan Museum of Art, 1000 Fifth Ave, Gallery 899, Manhattan
events.why: Not the predictable Pollock retrospective — framed as a dual study of two artists sharing a life and a practice, it's really about how proximity, ego, influence, and domestic labor shape a body of work; opens this weekend.

events.name: Salon Art + Design — 15th Edition
events.venue: Park Avenue Armory, 643 Park Ave, Manhattan
events.why: The best version of a design fair in New York — collectible furniture, ceramics, antiquities, and 20th-century art in the same room; less art-world theater than Frieze, more actual objects worth thinking about.
